doordash-fees-for-restaurants.html.text:
← Delivery app margin calculator

How much does DoorDash take from restaurants?

“DoorDash takes 30%” is the wrong unit. The commission is a percentage of the order, but packaging and the extra minutes to bag a delivery ticket are cash you spend either way — and the listed price on the app is often still the dine-in price. Here is one ticket worked through both paths, with every number visible.

The ticket

A $32 check. Food cost is $9.60. Extra bagging time is eight minutes at $18/hour ($2.40). Delivery packaging is $1.25. Same food, same kitchen — only the path changes.

Dine-in

No marketplace commission. Card processing is usually the only platform fee. Using an illustrative 2.9% + $0.30:

Illustrative rates. Yours depend on your processor — check a recent batch.
Ticket$32.00
Card processing, 2.9% of $32 + $0.30−$1.23
Food cost−$9.60
You keep$21.17

DoorDash at the same $32

Marketplace commission is usually billed on the order total and often includes payment processing. Using an illustrative 27%, plus the packaging and bagging time dine-in did not need:

Illustrative 27% marketplace plan. Replace it with the rate on your payout statement.
Listed price$32.00
Commission, 27% of $32−$8.64
Food cost−$9.60
Packaging−$1.25
Eight extra minutes at $18/hour−$2.40
You keep$10.11

The gap, and the price that closes it

On this ticket DoorDash leaves $11.06 less than dine-in. At 400 such orders a month that is $4,424 — before refunds, promotions, or the dine-in seats you did not fill because the kitchen was bagging.

To keep the same $21.17 as dine-in, the DoorDash listed price has to cover commission and the extra cash. The algebra is:

($21.17 + $13.25) ÷ (1 − 0.27) = $47.15

That is a 47% markup on the dine-in ticket, not a 27% one. A restaurant that marks delivery up by the commission percentage alone still loses packaging, labor, and the commission on the markup.

Why this is not “stop using DoorDash”

The app may be selling tickets you would not have sold. $10.11 on an incremental order is still $10.11. The comparison tells you what each path leaves, and what you have to charge to make them equal — not whether the demand is incremental. Put your own rates into the calculator before treating any of these numbers as yours.

Common questions

How much does DoorDash take from restaurants?

The marketplace commission is a percentage of the order, usually billed on the order total and often including payment processing. On a $32 ticket at an illustrative 27% that is $8.64, but the commission is not the whole cost: delivery packaging and the extra minutes to bag a delivery ticket are cash you spend on top of it. In the worked example the DoorDash path leaves $10.11 against $21.17 for the same ticket dine-in.

How much should a restaurant mark up delivery prices?

Enough to cover the commission and the extra cash, not the commission percentage alone. In the worked example, keeping the same $21.17 as dine-in needs $21.17 plus $13.25, divided by 1 minus 0.27, which is $47.15 on a $32 dine-in ticket. That is a 47% markup, not a 27% one.

doordash-vs-ubereats-fees.html.text:
← Delivery app margin calculator

DoorDash vs Uber Eats fees on the same ticket

“DoorDash takes 30%, Uber Eats takes 30%” pages treat every delivery app as interchangeable. The commission rates are not identical, and a few points of difference compounds over hundreds of orders a month. Here is one ticket worked through all three apps, with every number visible.

The ticket

A $32 check. Food cost is $9.60. Extra bagging time is eight minutes at $18/hour ($2.40). Delivery packaging is $1.25. Same food, same kitchen, same listed price — only the app changes.

DoorDash

Marketplace commission is usually billed on the order total and often includes payment processing. Using an illustrative 27%:

Illustrative 27% marketplace plan. Replace it with the rate on your payout statement.
Listed price$32.00
Commission, 27% of $32−$8.64
Food cost−$9.60
Packaging−$1.25
Eight extra minutes at $18/hour−$2.40
You keep$10.11

Uber Eats

Commission is typically a percentage of the order too, and some plans add a separate processing fee on top. Using an illustrative 30%, with the same packaging and bagging time DoorDash needed:

Illustrative 30% marketplace plan. Some plans bill payment processing separately — add it in the calculator if yours does.
Listed price$32.00
Commission, 30% of $32−$9.60
Food cost−$9.60
Packaging−$1.25
Eight extra minutes at $18/hour−$2.40
You keep$9.15

Grubhub

Commission varies by plan and market more than the other two — using an illustrative 25%, still with the same packaging and labor:

Illustrative 25% bundled commission. Split out marketing or delivery add-ons if your plan bills them separately.
Listed price$32.00
Commission, 25% of $32−$8.00
Food cost−$9.60
Packaging−$1.25
Eight extra minutes at $18/hour−$2.40
You keep$10.75

The ranking, and what it costs monthly

On this ticket the order is Grubhub ($10.75) > DoorDash ($10.11) > Uber Eats ($9.15) — a $1.60 spread between the best and worst app on one order. At 400 such orders a month, choosing Uber Eats over Grubhub costs $640; choosing it over DoorDash costs $384. None of that is a claim about which app sells more tickets — see below.

Listed price each app needs to keep the same $21.17 as dine-in on this ticket.
DoorDash (27% commission)$47.15
Uber Eats (30% commission)$49.17
Grubhub (25% commission)$45.89

The higher the commission, the higher the delivery menu has to be marked up to match dine-in — not because the app is doing anything different with packaging or labor, but because a bigger percentage cut needs a bigger price to leave the same cash behind it.

Why the ranking isn't fixed

Three things move it that this worked example holds constant:

  • Commission plans vary by restaurant, market, and tier. A restaurant on a marketing-inclusive plan can pay a materially higher rate than the illustrative ones above; a small independent and a chain can see different numbers from the same app.
  • Some apps bill payment processing separately. This example assumes all three bundle it into commission, which is common but not universal — split it out in the calculator if your statement shows a separate line.
  • Order volume is not the same across apps. An app with a higher commission that brings three times the orders can still be worth more in total than a cheaper one with little traffic. The per-ticket gap above is one input, not the whole decision.

Put your own commission rates, packaging cost, and order volume for each app into the calculator before treating any ranking as yours — including this one.

Common questions

Is DoorDash or Uber Eats cheaper for a restaurant?

On the same $32 ticket with illustrative commission of 27% for DoorDash and 30% for Uber Eats, DoorDash keeps $10.11 against Uber Eats' $9.15 — a $0.96 gap per order that comes entirely from the 3-point difference in commission, since packaging and labor are modeled the same on both. At 400 such orders a month that is $384, before either app's actual plan or promotions are counted.

Does Grubhub really charge less than DoorDash and Uber Eats?

In this worked example, yes: an illustrative 25% commission leaves $10.75 on the same $32 ticket, ahead of both DoorDash ($10.11) and Uber Eats ($9.15). But commission plans on all three apps vary by market, restaurant size, and whether marketing or priority placement is bundled in — replace these illustrative rates with the numbers on your own payout statements before trusting the ranking.

A single-app version of this walkthrough, against dine-in, is on doordash-fees-for-restaurants.html.

FOR INDEPENDENT RESTAURANTS AND CAFES

One ticket. Every path. See what DoorDash actually leaves you.

Enter a typical ticket once. This compares what dine-in, pickup, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, and your own driver each leave after commission, card processing, packaging, and the extra minutes to bag a delivery order — and tells you the delivery-menu price each app needs to match dine-in. Everything runs in this page; nothing is uploaded.

Your ticket

These apply to every path. A higher DoorDash menu price, extra packaging, or your own driver cost goes in that path’s panel below the table.

Path Listed Fees You keep Vs dine-in Price to match dine-in Commission to match dine-in This month vs dine-in

Transparent arithmetic from the rates you entered — not any app’s current published schedule. Commissions vary by plan, market, and contract. Check yours against a recent payout statement.

Each path’s rates and costs

Opened defaults are illustrative US rates, not a live fee schedule. Replace them with the rates on your own statements — that is what makes the comparison yours rather than a generic estimate.

What this does, and what it does not

The headline commission is not the decision

A 27% DoorDash plan on a $32 ticket is $8.64. Packaging and eight extra bagging minutes at $18/hour add another $3.65 the percentage comparison never shows. The decision number is the listed price that leaves you the same cash as dine-in — often around 45% higher on that ticket — and the monthly gap if you do not raise it. Since you cannot always set that price yourself, the table also solves the other side: the commission rate this path would need, at its current listed price, to match dine-in — the number worth having ready when a plan renewal or a lower-commission tier comes up. DoorDash fees on one restaurant ticket works the default example through in full, and DoorDash vs Uber Eats fees lines the three delivery apps up against each other on the same ticket.

What it deliberately leaves out

Fees are not the whole decision. An app fee is partly a payment for demand you would otherwise have to create, and this page has no way to know how many of those tickets you would have sold as dine-in or pickup. It also does not model refunds, marketing credits, DashPass discounts you absorb, or occupancy you lose when the kitchen is full of delivery tickets. Read the gap as one input, not the decision. It does not recommend a price, a contract, or a business model, and it is not tax, financial, or business advice.

Common questions

How much does DoorDash take from restaurants?

It depends on the plan and market. Marketplace commissions commonly land between about 15% and 30% of the order total, and some plans add a separate processing fee. The number that matters is not the headline percentage: packaging, extra bagging minutes, and the price you list on the app all change what you keep. Enter the rate on your own statement above — this page does the arithmetic on the numbers you give it.

Is DoorDash worth it for a restaurant?

On fees alone, dine-in almost always leaves more than a marketplace order at the same menu price, because the app takes a commission dine-in does not. Whether that is worth it depends on whether the app brings tickets you would not have sold otherwise, and on whether you mark the delivery menu up enough to keep the same cash. This calculator shows the dine-in-matching price and the monthly gap; it does not know your incremental demand.

How do I price a DoorDash menu to keep dine-in profit?

Take the profit you keep on the dine-in ticket, add packaging, extra labor, and any separate processing fee, then divide by one minus the commission rate. The last columns of the table do that from the rates you entered. A worked example is on the DoorDash fees page linked below.

How much does Uber Eats take from restaurants?

Like DoorDash, Uber Eats commission depends on the plan and market, and commonly lands in a similar rough range of the order total, sometimes with a separate marketing or processing fee depending on the tier. The Uber Eats preset above starts at 30% as an illustrative default — replace it with the rate on your own statement, then this page shows the same dine-in-matching price and monthly gap it computes for DoorDash.

How much commission does Grubhub charge restaurants?

Grubhub's commission also varies by plan and market, and is often bundled with marketing or delivery fees rather than one flat number. The Grubhub preset above starts at 25% as an illustrative default. Enter your own statement's rate to see the menu price Grubhub needs to match dine-in profit on this ticket, and how that compares to DoorDash and Uber Eats side by side.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Delivery App Margin Calculator

Delivery App Margin Calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A spreadsheet multiplies a ticket by a commission rate fine — once you have written a formula for every channel's fee shape, and a second one, solved backwards, for the price or commission rate that matches dine-in. This page has both built in.

What each does

A restaurant's own spreadsheet can absolutely hold a ticket price, a commission rate, and a formula that multiplies them. That arithmetic is trivial and correct once every cell already has the right formula in it. What it does not do on its own is apply a different fee shape per channel: dine-in and pickup pay card processing only, a marketplace's commission is often a percentage that bundles payment processing while some plans split the two into separate rates, and packaging plus extra bagging minutes at your hourly wage are cash the restaurant spends on every delivery ticket whether or not the app takes a cut. Six channels, six fee shapes, six formulas to keep in sync as any one rate changes.

This calculator carries those six fee shapes built in. Enter one ticket's price, food cost, packaging cost, hourly wage, and the commission and processing rates from your own statements, and it reports what dine-in, pickup, each delivery app, and your own driver keep after fees — plus, solved for you rather than by hand, the delivery-menu price that would match dine-in profit on that ticket, the commission rate a channel would need at its current price to match it, and the monthly cash gap if you change neither. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What's a ticket times a commission percentage?Either one — a spreadsheet multiplies fine, once the formula is written.
Does this channel's fee apply to the listed price, and is processing bundled in or separate?This calculator — each channel's commission, payment rate, and fixed fee are applied on the same defined base automatically; a spreadsheet needs a correct formula per channel and no drift between them.
What do packaging and extra bagging minutes add, in dollars?This calculator — packaging cost plus labor minutes times your hourly wage, computed per channel; a spreadsheet needs its own formula and an hourly-wage cell kept current.
What delivery-menu price matches what I'd keep dine-in on the same ticket?This calculator's own column — the fee formula solved backwards for price, not a flat markup guess or a manual goal-seek.
What commission rate would this app need, at today's listed price, to match dine-in?This calculator — the same formula solved backwards for rate instead of price, ready for a plan-renewal conversation.
What is the monthly cash gap if I change nothing?This calculator — the per-ticket gap times your expected monthly order count for that channel.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No, on either — but this calculator needs no template, no formula to write, and nothing to keep in sync across six channels' cells.

A spreadsheet is still the right tool for an ongoing monthly P&L across every channel over a year. This page answers one narrower question at a time — what does today's ticket actually keep on each channel, and what price or rate would match dine-in — and nothing it computes is saved anywhere once you leave the page.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, your entries are saved to this browser's local storage only, and nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't a delivery app's cut just the ticket times a commission percentage?

The multiplication itself is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine once you already know the commission rate. What a plain spreadsheet does not do on its own is apply a different fee shape per channel — dine-in and pickup pay card processing only, a marketplace commission is often bundled with payment processing while some plans split them, and packaging cost plus extra bagging minutes at your hourly wage are cash the restaurant spends whether or not the app takes a cut. Six channels, six formulas, kept in sync as any one rate changes.

Will a spreadsheet tell me the delivery-menu price that matches dine-in profit?

Not without solving the fee formula backwards, which most spreadsheets used for this are not set up to do. Profit is price minus commission minus processing minus packaging minus labor minus food cost; the price that reproduces a target profit is that equation rearranged for price, and the algebra changes depending on whether the fee is a straight percentage or has a fixed component too. This calculator solves it directly for every channel and also reports the commission rate a channel would need, at its current listed price, to match dine-in — the number worth having ready when a plan renewal comes up.

What happens if I mix up which fees apply to the listed price versus the payout?

Nothing catches it — a spreadsheet returns whatever the formula says, whether the commission and processing rates you wired in apply to the right base or not. This calculator applies each channel's commission, payment rate, and fixed fee to the same defined base for every channel, so a rate typed into the wrong cell in a spreadsheet cannot silently understate or overstate what one channel keeps relative to another.

Does this replace a restaurant's own P&L or accounting spreadsheet?

No. A spreadsheet or accounting system that tracks every day's sales, costs, and margin across a full month or year is still the right tool for that ongoing record. This page answers one narrower question at a time — what does today's ticket actually keep on each channel, and what price or commission rate would match dine-in — and nothing it computes is saved anywhere once you leave the page.

vs-toast.html.text:
← Delivery App Margin Calculator

Delivery App Margin Calculator vs. Toast

Two different shapes: Toast is a point-of-sale platform a restaurant runs its whole operation through, every day, as an ongoing account. This page is a free worksheet for one ticket at a time — what a delivery app actually leaves you, and what price matches dine-in — before any POS system is involved.

What each tool is for

Toast is a cloud-based restaurant point-of-sale and management platform, publicly documented as covering order taking, payments, menu management, and reporting across a restaurant's dine-in, online ordering, and third-party delivery channels. It is an account-based platform, sold as an ongoing subscription together with point-of-sale hardware, not a one-off calculator. Toast's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — restaurant point-of-sale and management software, sold as a subscription with hardware — are stated, and no dollar amount for Toast appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Toast does. It does not take an order, process a payment, or reconcile a delivery app's payout against a bank deposit. It takes one ticket's price, food cost, hourly wage for extra bagging, and expected monthly delivery-order count, plus the commission, payment-processing, packaging, and delivery-cost rates from a DoorDash, Uber Eats, or Grubhub statement, and shows what dine-in, pickup, each delivery app, and your own driver leave after fees — plus the delivery-menu price and the commission rate each app would need to match dine-in profit on that ticket, and the monthly cash gap if you do not adjust. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I run a restaurant and need one system for orders, payments, and reporting across dine-in and delivery.Toast, or a comparable POS platform — running that system is not something this calculator does.
What does today's DoorDash, Uber Eats, or Grubhub ticket actually leave me, once packaging and extra labor are counted?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
What delivery-menu price matches what I'd keep from the same ticket dine-in?This calculator's "price to match dine-in" column, not a flat markup guess.
How does DoorDash's commission compare with Uber Eats' on the same ticket?This calculator's own DoorDash vs Uber Eats fees page.
I need one account so my whole staff is taking orders and running reports the same way.Toast, or a comparable POS platform.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Toast is used through a subscription account with hardware.

Most restaurants get different value from each: Toast (or a comparable POS platform) for running orders, payments, and reporting across every channel as an ongoing account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one ticket on one delivery app actually leaves before a POS system or a plan renewal is involved. This page's own figures are arithmetic from the rates you enter, not a live fee schedule, a payout reconciliation, or business advice.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, your entries are saved to this browser's local storage only, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Toast?

They answer different questions, and a restaurant may end up using both. Toast is a cloud-based restaurant point-of-sale and management platform, publicly documented as covering order taking, payments, and reporting across a restaurant's dine-in, online, and delivery channels, sold as an ongoing subscription with hardware. This calculator does one narrower thing: it takes a single ticket's price, food cost, and packaging and labor costs, and the commission and fee rates from your DoorDash, Uber Eats, or Grubhub statement, and shows what each path actually keeps after fees, plus the delivery-menu price that would match dine-in profit on that same ticket. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A restaurant that wants one system running its point of sale, payments, and channel reporting needs Toast or a comparable POS; someone deciding whether today's delivery commission is eating a ticket's profit is in the right place here.

Does this calculator replace restaurant reporting or a point-of-sale system?

No. It does not take orders, process payments, or reconcile a delivery app's payout against your bank deposit. It takes numbers you already have — a ticket's price and costs, and the fee rates from a statement — and computes what each channel keeps and the price that matches dine-in. Running orders, payments, and channel reporting day to day is a POS system's job, not a calculator's.

Is this page affiliated with Toast?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Toast, Inc. Toast is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.
